newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Parliament tackles Taiwan reserve requirements.
newsitem.headline: Parliament tackles Taiwan reserve requirements.

text.p: A joint committee of Taiwan's parliament has proposed a revision of the Central Bank Law that would allow the bank to enforce lower bank reserve requirements, officials said on Tuesday.
Under the draft revision, the legal range of reserve requirements for cheque deposits would be five percent to 25 percent, down from 15-40 percent, a central bank official said.

The legal range for passbook deposits would fall to 5-25 percent from 10-35 percent, while that for savings deposits would fall to 3-15 percent from 5-20 percent. The range for time deposits would fall to 3-15 percent from 7-25 percent.
The central bank would have discretion to adjust reserve requirements for all banks within the range limits.
The revision differed from the central bank's own draft, which proposed scrapping the specified range limits altogether to improve Taiwan's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.
"The joint committee set the new range limits because legislators do not want to see a central bank that is too powerful," a parliament aide said by telephone.
The revision must be approved by the full parliament before it can become law.
The panel agreed to scrap limits on banks' foreign liabilities outstanding, but set a new 5-25 percent range limit for reserve requirements on banks' liabilities other than desposits, the aide said.

The Economic Daily News estimated the new limits on liabilities, if enacted, would oblige the central bank to tighten liquidity by at least T$35 billion to ensure the market is not flooded by newly liberated cash reserves.
The paper quoted unnamed central bank officials as saying the bank would try to persuade parliament to resurrect its original draft when the issue comes before the full body.
The bank had said its draft would afford the central bank more flexible operations, in accord with global trends.

For example, officials said, if reserve requirement range limits were scrapped altogether, the central bank could when necessary impose a 100 percent reserve requirement on inflowing "hot money" to prevent a destabilising flood into local markets.
The central bank had repeatedly said it would gradually lower banks' reserve requirements at the "appropriate time", but has not said when or to what degree this would be done.
